opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it is fairly simple, at least conceptually. Full automation means AI systems can do essentially every task that humans currently get paid to do in the economy, and do it at least as well and at a cost that's competitive with hiring a human. That last part matters a lot. It's not enough for a system to be technically capable of doing something if it costs a hundred times more than a person. The economically relevant question is whether, when an employer is deciding who or what should do a job, AI is the better choice across basically the whole range of work.

And I want to stress that this covers both cognitive and physical work. A lot of discussion focuses on remote work, the kinds of things you can do on a computer, like writing code, analyzing data, or answering customer emails. That's a big chunk of the economy, but it's far from all of it. You also have construction, manufacturing, caregiving, plumbing, agriculture, and so on. Full automation in my sense requires robotics that are good enough and cheap enough to handle that physical work, not just language models that are good at software.

A useful way to see this is to ask what fraction of current labor income could be captured by AI systems. If we get to the point where AI can do remote work tasks but not physical ones, maybe that's something like a third or a half of the economy in rich countries. That's enormous, but it's not full automation. The remaining tasks become bottlenecks: wages for them rise, and the economy can't grow arbitrarily fast because you're still constrained by human labor in those areas.

Another subtle point is that jobs are bundles of tasks, and automation usually happens task by task rather than job by job. A job might be ninety percent automatable, but if the remaining ten percent requires a human, you still need that human. So full automation means having no such residual tasks left, with nothing in the production process where you need a human in the loop for capability reasons. There may still be things people want humans to do for their own sake, like watching human athletes or getting care from a person, but that's a matter of preference rather than necessity.

So in short: AI and robotics that can substitute for human labor across essentially all economically valuable tasks, cognitive and physical, at competitive cost. That's the threshold where I'd expect really dramatic changes in economic growth rates, because labor stops being a binding constraint.

r001.rationale: The response defines full automation as covering essentially all economically valuable work and explains that remaining human tasks constrain growth by becoming bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I usually think about it is in terms of the tasks that are economically valuable in the economy today. So if you look at something like the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupation data, there's this long list of tasks that workers do, and the question is: can AI systems do essentially all of those tasks, at a cost and a quality level that's competitive with human workers? That's what I would call full automation.

And I think it's important to be precise about this, because people often conflate it with things like "AI can write code" or "AI can pass some exam." Those are impressive, but they're a very small slice of what the economy actually consists of. A lot of economically valuable work involves things like physical manipulation, long-horizon planning, coordinating with other people, dealing with messy and underspecified situations where nobody tells you what the task even is. So when I say full automation, I mean the AI can substitute for human labor across basically the entire distribution of those tasks, not just the ones that happen to be easy to benchmark.

There's also a subtlety around whether you count physical tasks. I think you have to, because something like a third or more of the value in the economy is tied to work that requires a body, and the point at which robotics catches up with cognitive capabilities could be quite different. So you can talk about "full automation of remote work" as a separate milestone, and that's a meaningful thing, but it's not the same as full automation of labor.

The other thing I'd say is that it's not really about whether the AI can do a task in principle. It's about whether it's actually cheaper or better than hiring a person, so that firms substitute. That's what determines the economic effects, like growth acceleration or wage effects. You could imagine a world where AI is technically capable of everything but the inference cost is so high that it only displaces a fraction of jobs, and I wouldn't call that full automation yet. So the definition has an economic component and a capabilities component, and both have to be satisfied.

r001.rationale: It defines full automation as AI competitively substituting for human labor across essentially all economically valuable tasks, including physical work. It does not state that the defining set is tasks whose remaining unautomated would bottleneck GDP.

astra-6.text:
I’d define full automation as AI being able to perform essentially all the tasks that humans currently do for economic purposes. That includes both cognitive work and physical work, so it’s not just a question of what a model can do on a computer. You also need robotics capable of operating in the real world.

And there’s an economic condition: being able to do a task at some enormous cost isn’t enough. The system needs to do it reliably, at a comparable level of quality, and cheaply enough that replacing human labor makes economic sense. That doesn’t mean humans stop working entirely. People might still value something specifically because a human made it, or work because they enjoy it. It means human labor is no longer necessary to perform those tasks.

r001.rationale: The response defines full automation as performing essentially all tasks humans do for economic purposes, but it does not specify that the remaining unautomated tasks would create a bottleneck on GDP.

sol-6.1.text:
I would define full automation as AI being able to perform essentially all the tasks that humans currently do to produce goods and services. That includes physical work, so you need robotics as well as systems that can do things on a computer. And it includes the work of coming up with new ideas, doing research, and developing better technologies.

The relevant standard is economic: can you substitute an AI system for a human worker at comparable quality and at a competitive cost? A system might be capable of doing a task, but if it costs much more than employing a person, that doesn’t give you automation in the economically meaningful sense.

That doesn’t mean AI has to do absolutely everything a human could possibly do. It means that human labor is no longer necessary for the productive tasks that keep the economy running and allow it to grow.

r001.rationale: The response says full automation removes the need for human labor in productive tasks that keep the economy running and allow it to grow, which conveys automating tasks whose absence would constrain economic output.
